paraphrase: Frame dialogue. The Goddess says she has heard the whole Trika from the Rudrayāmala and still doubts what Bhairava's form is in truth: the mass of sounds, the ninefold, the three-headed, the three powers, nāda-bindu, and so on; she argues that supremacy cannot belong to what has parts (1-6). Bhairava answers that the forms with parts are unsubstantial, given for meditation to the confused and as an inducement to engage (7-13); the supreme state is unspeakable, free of direction, time and place, blissful, thought-free and full, and is the Goddess Parā, not different from power as fire is not from its burning (14-21). The Goddess asks by what means it is entered (22-23).

paraphrase: The means (the dhāraṇās, in the skeleton's word), given by Bhairava in answer to the Goddess: 115 verse-segments in the GRETIL numbering, counted as a hundred and twelve teachings of the waveless state at v.139. They begin at the breath (24-27) and rising power (28-31, restricted), then voids and sounds (32-42), the body as space (43-51), burning of body and world (52-53), dissolving the principles and the universe (54-60), the middle between two states (61-62), consciousness and bliss (63-74), the threshold of sleep, gazing, seals and postures (75-85), darkness and sounds (86-91), space and desire (92-99), the same consciousness in all and steadying the understanding (100-110), forcing methods (111, 113-114) and thought-free absorption (112, 115-122), then equality, supportless space and the mind that does not stay (123-138).

paraphrase: Closing. The means are summed as a hundred and twelve teachings of the waveless state, knowing which one becomes a knower of knowledge; established in any one, one becomes Bhairava, released while living (139-142). Asked who is repeated, meditated on, worshipped and satisfied, Bhairava redefines japa, meditation, worship, oblation, sacrifice and bathing as inner acts (143-153), describes the Goddess's natural movement as breath (154-156), forbids revealing the teaching except to worthy recipients (157-160), and the Goddess, satisfied that she has ascertained the essence of the Rudrayāmala, embraces Śiva (161-162).

paraphrase: Thesis, decided by the six marks. The text presents Bhairava's supreme state, which is also the Goddess Parā, as unspeakable fullness, free of direction, time and place and not any of the forms with parts (vv.7-21), and offers, as the means of entering it, a run of short contemplations of the waveless state (24-138), each turning the mind to something in ordinary experience (a breath, a void, a sound's end, the middle between two states, joy, the thought that all is consciousness) or away from the mind's supports; established in any one of them one becomes Bhairava (140), and the outer acts of worship are to be understood as these inner acts (144-153). Marks. Opening and closing (upakrama/upasaṃhāra): opens with the Goddess's question about Bhairava's form (1-6) and closes with her statement that the essence of the Rudrayāmala has been ascertained (161-162). Repetition (abhyāsa): the refrains of the thought-free (nirvikalpa), the supportless (nirādhāra), the void (śūnya), 'made of it' (tanmaya), endings on 'Bhairava's form' (84, 112, 138) and 'wherever the mind goes' (116, 129). Novelty (apūrvatā): 'the essence of tantra, most secret' (7-8, 157). Stated result (phala): 140-142 and 148, and a result at the end of most verses. Praise (arthavāda): 141, 156 ('easy'), 157-160. Reasoned demonstration (upapatti): 5-6 (supremacy is contradicted by having parts), 18-19 (power and fire), 110 (waves and water), 134-137, 152-153.
